The [government of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Government of the People's Republic of China") does not release exact unified statistics on crime rates and the rate of criminal offending. Scarce official statistics released are the subject of much academic debate due to allegations of statistical fabrication, under-reporting and corruption.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) The illegal drug trade in China is a significant driver of violent crime, including murder.

According to the [Global Organized Crime Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Organized_Crime_Index "Global Organized Crime Index") (2023), China is grappling with deep-seated criminal activities across diverse markets, while its resilience is limited by [corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption "Corruption") and the centralized control of governance and [information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information "Information").[[3]](#cite_note-GOCI-3)

A distinguishing feature of the [Qin dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_dynasty "Qin dynasty") was its treatment of criminals: harsh but careful and fair.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[*[contentious label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:LABEL "Wikipedia:LABEL")*] Succeeding dynasties moderated the law in various ways. In the [Ming dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_dynasty "Ming dynasty"), commercialization and urbanization meant that scams abounded.[[5]](#cite_note-:0-5) [Fences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fences_in_Ming_China "Fences in Ming China") who disposed of stolen goods thrived.[[5]](#cite_note-:0-5) The People's Republic of China (PRC) was established in 1949 and, from 1949 to 1956, underwent the process of transferring the [means of production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Means_of_production "Means of production") to [common ownership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_ownership "Common ownership").[[6]](#cite_note-CCCP241-6) During this time, the new government worked to decrease the influence of criminal gangs[[7]](#cite_note-7) and reduce the prevalence of narcotics[[6]](#cite_note-CCCP241-6) and gambling.[[8]](#cite_note-CCCP242-8) Efforts to crack down on criminal activity by the government led to a decrease in crime.[[8]](#cite_note-CCCP242-8)

Between 1949 and 1956, larceny, arson, rape, murder, and robbery were major nonpolitical offenses.[[8]](#cite_note-CCCP242-8) The majority of economic crimes were committed by business people who engaged in tax evasion, theft of public property, and [bribery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bribery "Bribery").[[8]](#cite_note-CCCP242-8)

Government officials also engaged in illegal economic activity, which included improperly taking public property and accepting bribes.[[8]](#cite_note-CCCP242-8) Between 1957 and 1965, rural areas experienced little reported crime.[[8]](#cite_note-CCCP242-8) Crime rates increased later. The year 1981 represented a peak in reported crime.[[9]](#cite_note-CPPC64-9) This may have been correlated to the [reform and opening up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_and_opening_up "Reform and opening up") from 1978, which allowed some elements of a [market economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_economy "Market economy") and gave rise to an increase in economic activity.[[9]](#cite_note-CPPC64-9) Below is a comparison of reported cases of crime from 1977 to 1988 (excluding economic crimes):[[10]](#cite_note-CCCP245-10)

Death of Li Keqiang

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Li Keqiang in January 2023 | |
| Date | 27 October – 2 November 2023 |
| Location | * [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") |

[Li Keqiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Keqiang "Li Keqiang"), former [premier of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Premier of the People's Republic of China") and member of the [17th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th_Politburo_Standing_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "17th Politburo Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party"), [18th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_Politburo_Standing_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "18th Politburo Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party"), and [19th Politburo Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_Politburo_Standing_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "19th Politburo Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party"), died on 27 October 2023 at 00:10 CST in Shanghai, aged 68.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Li Keqiang became the youngest Premier at the time of leaving office and the earliest to die among all Premiers since the 1949 [proclamation of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Proclamation of the People's Republic of China").[[2]](#cite_note-voanews2023-11-02-2)

### Resignations from party and governmental positions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Death_of_Li_Keqiang&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Resignations from party and governmental positions")]

After the [first plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_plenary_session_of_the_20th_Central_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "First plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party") in October 2022, Li resigned from his [party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") roles, including his membership of the Politburo Standing Committee. Following the first session of the [14th National People's Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/14th_National_People's_Congress "14th National People's Congress"), he also stepped down as Premier, retiring from public office at the age of 67.

After his official retirement, Li maintained a low profile, did not participate in official affairs, and rarely appeared in public. On 30 August 2023, Li visited the [Mogao Caves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mogao_Caves "Mogao Caves") in [Dunhuang, Gansu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunhuang "Dunhuang"); this was his final public appearance.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

According to the 2010 biography *He Will Be China's Chief Steward: A Biography of Li Keqiang*, Li suffered from severe [myocarditis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myocarditis "Myocarditis") during his time at [Peking University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_University "Peking University") due to overexertion. He frequently experienced [shortness of breath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortness_of_breath "Shortness of breath") during physically strenuous activities.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Reports also indicated that Li had [diabetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabetes "Diabetes"), which was further exacerbated by his demanding domestic and diplomatic work.[[5]](#cite_note-voachinese.com-5) Cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases caused by [atherosclerosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atherosclerosis "Atherosclerosis") is a common complication and leading cause of death among diabetes patients.[[6]](#cite_note-uptodate.com-6)

The *[South China Morning Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Morning_Post "South China Morning Post")* reported that Li Keqiang had previously had [heart bypass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_artery_bypass_surgery "Coronary artery bypass surgery") surgery.[[7]](#cite_note-南华-7)

Li suffered a sudden heart attack while swimming at the *Shanghai Dongjiao Hotel* on 26 October 2023.[[7]](#cite_note-南华-7) He was accompanied by his wife [Cheng Hong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheng_Hong "Cheng Hong").[[8]](#cite_note-8) It was reported that the heart attack occurred around noon on 26 October. Li Keqiang was rushed to the Shanghai Shuguang Hospital (East Campus)[[9]](#cite_note-scmp.com-9) by security and medical personnel after the incident. All available resources were mobilized,[[10]](#cite_note-10) including top experts from Shanghai and the installation of an [extracorporeal membrane oxygenation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extracorporeal_membrane_oxygenation "Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation") (ECMO) device that afternoon. Despite emergency rescue efforts lasting over 10 hours, medical teams were unable to save him. Li died at 12:10 a.m. the next day.

In 2014, the [administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping_Administration "Xi Jinping Administration") of [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) [general secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") launched the [Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_Hard_Campaign_Against_Violent_Terrorism "Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism"), which involved surveillance and restrictions in Xinjiang. **Peng Lifa** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 彭立发; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Péng Lìfā*; born January 7, 1974[[1]](#cite_note-DW_2024-1)) is a Chinese [democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_movements_of_China "Democracy movements of China") activist who initiated the [Beijing Sitong Bridge protest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Sitong_Bridge_protest "Beijing Sitong Bridge protest") in October 2022 before the [20th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_National_Congress_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "20th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party"). He was named one of the [100 most influential people in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100") by *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")* magazine in 2023.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

## Career and activism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Peng_Lifa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career and activism")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A9%8B%E6%8A%97%E8%AD%B0%E8%80%85%E8%A2%AB%E5%B8%B6%E4%B8%8A%E8%AD%A6%E8%BB%8A.png/250px-%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A9%8B%E6%8A%97%E8%AD%B0%E8%80%85%E8%A2%AB%E5%B8%B6%E4%B8%8A%E8%AD%A6%E8%BB%8A.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A9%8B%E6%8A%97%E8%AD%B0%E8%80%85%E8%A2%AB%E5%B8%B6%E4%B8%8A%E8%AD%A6%E8%BB%8A.png)

Peng (dressed in orange) was brought into a police vehicle, on Sitong Bridge.

Peng worked for an acrylic products firm called Beijing Melon Network Technology Co., Ltd.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) He wrote articles on [electromagnetism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetism "Electromagnetism").[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5)

On October 13, 2022, Peng initiated the [Beijing Sitong Bridge protest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Sitong_Bridge_protest "Beijing Sitong Bridge protest") by posting a banner on the [Sitong Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitong_Bridge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sitong Bridge (page does not exist)") [[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A1%A5 "zh:四通桥")].[[6]](#cite_note-:0-6) Peng draped protest banners from Beijing's Sitong Bridge. They unfurled to reveal exhortations against China's [zero-COVID policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-COVID_policy "Zero-COVID policy"), calling it a violation of freedom of expression and demanding real elections and political reform.

Peng further challenged [General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") on October 13, 2022, by shouting through a loudspeaker, "We want to eat. We want freedom. We want votes!." He is suspected to have been detained by the police.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) His slogans spread across the country with comparisons being made between Peng and the [Tank Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tank_Man "Tank Man").[[6]](#cite_note-:0-6) His act was described by [BBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_News "BBC News") as "one of the most significant acts of Chinese protest seen under [Xi's rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_secretaryship_of_Xi_Jinping "General secretaryship of Xi Jinping")."[[7]](#cite_note-bbc-7)

Though the *[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* published an article on December 7, 2022, naming him "Peng Lifa," the protester's identity has not been confirmed.[[7]](#cite_note-bbc-7) However, some believe him to be an academic physicist and have flooded a Twitter account assumed to be linked to the protester with messages of admiration.[[7]](#cite_note-bbc-7) *[The Wall Street Jour

The **Beijing Sitong Bridge protest** was a protest that took place on October 13, 2022, in [Haidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haidian,_Beijing "Haidian, Beijing"), [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), China.

The protest happened three days before the opening of the [20th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_National_Congress_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "20th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party") (CCP). On the morning of October 13, 2022, a protester demonstrated against [CCP general secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping")'s [cult of personality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping's_cult_of_personality "Xi Jinping's cult of personality"), [dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_secretaryship_of_Xi_Jinping "General secretaryship of Xi Jinping"), [human rights violations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_China "Human rights in China"), strengthening of [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_China "Censorship in China"), seeking of [leadership for life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_for_life "President for life") and implementation of the [zero-COVID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-COVID "Zero-COVID") policy by hanging banners and burning tires on [Sitong Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitong_Bridge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sitong Bridge (page does not exist)") [[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A1%A5 "zh:四通桥")] ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 四通桥; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Sìtōng Qiáo*) in Haidian, Beijing.

The protester, [Peng Lifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peng_Lifa "Peng Lifa") (彭立发; pinyin: Péng Lìfā; b. 1974),[[1]](#cite_note-1) has been dubbed Bridge Man or Banner Man in reference to [Tank Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tank_Man "Tank Man").

Protests took place frequently in China in the 2000s, with 180,000 protests taking place in 2010 according to [Tsinghua University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsinghua_University "Tsinghua University") sociology professor Sun Liping.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

This protest against Xi Jinping and his policies was rare, as it came just days before the start of the CCP National Congress, a period during which the authorities imposed extremely tight control over protests and dissent. It was widely expected that Xi's rule for an unprecedented third term would be cemented at the Congress.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Events in the year **[2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023 "2023") in [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")**.

* [General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") – [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping")
* [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_China "President of China") – [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping")
* [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_China "Vice President of China")
  + [Wang Qishan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Qishan "Wang Qishan") (until 10 March 2023)
  + [Han Zheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Zheng "Han Zheng") (from 10 March 2023)
* [Premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_China "Premier of China")
  + [Li Keqiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Keqiang "Li Keqiang") (until 11 March 2023)
  + [Li Qiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Qiang "Li Qiang") (from 11 March 2023)
* [Congress chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Standing_Committee_of_the_National_People's_Congress "Chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress") – [Li Zhanshu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Zhanshu "Li Zhanshu")
* [Consultative Conference chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_National_Committee_of_the_Chinese_People's_Political_Consultative_Conference "Chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference") – [Wang Yang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Yang_(politician) "Wang Yang (politician)")
* [Supervision Commission director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_the_National_Supervisory_Commission "Director of the National Supervisory Commission") – [Yang Xiaodu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang_Xiaodu "Yang Xiaodu")

* 8 January – 17 people are killed and 22 others injured when a truck hits a [funeral procession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral_procession "Funeral procession") in [Nanchang County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanchang_County "Nanchang County"), [Jiangxi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiangxi "Jiangxi").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* 11 January – [2023 Guangzhou car attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Guangzhou_car_attack "2023 Guangzhou car attack"): Five people are killed and 13 others injured when a man [rams his vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle-ramming_attack "Vehicle-ramming attack") into a crowd in [Guangzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou "Guangzhou"), [Guangdong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangdong "Guangdong").[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* 17 January – [2023 Nyingchi avalanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Nyingchi_avalanche "2023 Nyingchi avalanche"): An [avalanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalanche "Avalanche") in [Nyingchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyingchi "Nyingchi"), [Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet"), kills 28 people.[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* 4 February – At least 16 people are killed and 66 others injured in a [multiple-vehicle collision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple-vehicle_collision "Multiple-vehicle collision") along a highway in [Changsha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changsha "Changsha")
